headline: Every stereo algorithm is the same four-stage pipeline — so compare stages, not whole systems.
summary: Scharstein & Szeliski turned stereo matching from a zoo of incomparable methods into a measurable science: a shared 4-step taxonomy, a testbed to swap one step at a time, and ground-truth data to score the result. For a robotics stereo system, that gives you both a design vocabulary and an evaluation method.

items.label: Journal version
items.hint: expanded from a 2001 IEEE workshop paper

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.subtitle: What matters most from your sources so far

items.title: Dense stereo = four interchangeable stages
items.body: Almost every two-frame algorithm can be decomposed into **matching cost**, **cost aggregation**, **disparity optimisation** and **refinement**. Describe any method you read in these four terms.

items.title: Improve one stage, hold the rest fixed
items.body: The paper's C++ testbed lets you swap a single stage (e.g. a new aggregation window) and measure the change in isolation — a clean experimental design you can copy for your own evaluation.

items.title: Ground truth made the field measurable
items.body: Accurate ground-truth disparity maps plus a public leaderboard replaced subjective "looks good" comparisons with error rates — arguably the paper's most lasting legacy.

items.title: Local vs global is the core design fork
items.body: Stage 3 is where methods split: pick the cheapest match per pixel (local), or solve for the whole disparity map at once (global — dynamic programming, graph cuts). This trade-off drives speed vs accuracy on a robot.

blocks.title: The stereo matching pipeline
blocks.subtitle: Scharstein & Szeliski's taxonomy — every dense method fits these steps

steps.label: Matching cost
steps.detail: Score how similar each left-image pixel is to candidate pixels in the right image.

steps.label: Cost aggregation
steps.detail: Sum or average costs over a local window to suppress noise and ambiguity.

steps.label: Disparity optimisation
steps.detail: Pick the best disparity per pixel — locally (winner-takes-all) or globally (DP, graph cuts).

steps.label: Refinement
steps.detail: Fix errors, fill occluded regions, and interpolate to sub-pixel precision.

blocks.title: Why this matters for your capstone
blocks.body: Your problem is **stereo vision systems in robotics**. Use the four-stage taxonomy to describe whatever system you build, and borrow the paper's evaluation style: fix three stages, vary one, and report error against ground truth. That turns "my depth map looks better" into a defensible result.

items.definition: Horizontal pixel shift of the same point between left and right images. Larger disparity = closer object; for rectified cameras depth is $Z = fB/d$.
A per-pixel similarity score between a left pixel and a candidate right pixel, e.g. absolute intensity difference.
Combining matching costs over a neighbourhood so single-pixel noise doesn't decide the match.
Regions visible to one camera but hidden from the other — they have no true match and must be filled in.
Interpolating between integer disparities to get smoother, more precise depth.
Exact, independently measured disparity maps used to score an algorithm's error rate.
